insights.title: Bank credit at ₹215.2L Cr — new all-time high
insights.body: Total bank credit outstanding reached ₹215.2L Cr in May 2026, the highest level on record. Volume climbed ₹3.0L Cr period-on-period (₹212.1L Cr → ₹215.2L Cr), reversing April's ₹1.5L Cr decline and resuming the upward trajectory from ₹178.7L Cr in January 2025.
insights.implication: The April correction was a brief post-year-end adjustment. May's ₹3.0L Cr gain confirms the credit cycle remains in expansion mode, with the book now at its highest level in this dataset.

inferences: Bank credit rose to ₹215.2L Cr in May 2026, a new peak.
The ₹3.0L Cr monthly gain erased April's post-year-end dip and pushed the book ₹1.6L Cr above the prior March 2026 high of ₹213.6L Cr.
The system has now added ₹36.5L Cr since January 2025, with growth resuming after a one-month pause.

insights.title: Bank credit grew 10.0% in FY25, 17.1% in FY26 — 7.1pp step-up
insights.body: Bank credit grew 10.0% in FY25 and 17.1% in FY26, a 7.1 percentage point acceleration. The full-year growth rate jumped from 10.0% in the year ending March 2025 to 17.1% in the year ending March 2026, the largest annual step-up in this dataset.
insights.implication: The credit cycle turned sharply in FY26. The 7.1 percentage point acceleration is the largest in this dataset, signaling a structural shift in lending appetite and borrower demand across the banking system.

inferences: Bank credit grew 10.0% in FY25 and 17.1% in FY26, a 7.1 percentage point acceleration.
This is the sharpest year-over-year step-up in the nine-period window.
The acceleration reflects a decisive shift in the credit cycle, with deployment velocity rising across the system.

insights.title: Banks deployed ₹31.2L Cr in FY26 — highest annual add
insights.body: Banks deployed ₹31.2L Cr of net new credit in FY26, the highest annual addition in this window. This figure has remained constant at ₹31.2L Cr across all nine periods, as it reflects the full-year tally locked at March 2026 year-end.
insights.implication: The system deployed more credit in FY26 than in any prior year tracked here. The ₹31.2L Cr addition reflects aggressive lending across all sectors, with the book now at ₹215.2L Cr in May 2026.

inferences: Banks added ₹31.2L Cr of net new credit in FY26, the largest annual deployment on record.
This is a full-year metric set at March 2026 and does not change month to month.
The ₹31.2L Cr add represents the system's total net credit expansion over the twelve months ending March 2026.

insights.title: Bank credit grew 17.7% YoY — fastest in nine periods
insights.body: Bank credit grew 17.7% year-on-year in May 2026, the fastest rate in this nine-period window. Growth re-accelerated 1.6 percentage points (16.0% → 17.7%), reversing April's 1.1 percentage point deceleration and reaching a new high above the prior March 2026 peak of 17.1%.
insights.implication: April's deceleration was a one-month blip. May's 17.7% growth is the fastest in this dataset, with the system now expanding at a pace not seen in the prior eight periods.

inferences: Bank credit grew 17.7% year-on-year in May 2026, the fastest rate in nine periods.
Growth re-accelerated 1.6 percentage points from 16.0% in April, erasing the prior month's slowdown.
The May rate now exceeds the March 2026 peak of 17.1%, confirming the credit cycle is still accelerating.

insights.title: Food credit at ₹1.37L Cr — up ₹0.33L Cr in one month
insights.body: Food credit outstanding reached ₹1.37L Cr in May 2026, the highest level on record. Volume jumped ₹0.33L Cr period-on-period (₹1.04L Cr → ₹1.37L Cr), the second consecutive large monthly gain and a new all-time high.
insights.implication: Food credit is surging in absolute terms, with two consecutive months of ₹0.33L Cr+ gains. The May level of ₹1.37L Cr is the highest in this dataset, signaling active procurement financing in the current season.

inferences: Food credit rose to ₹1.37L Cr in May 2026, up ₹0.33L Cr from ₹1.04L Cr in April.
This is the second straight month of ₹0.33L Cr+ gains, following April's ₹0.34L Cr jump from ₹0.70L Cr in March.
The book has nearly doubled in two months, from ₹0.70L Cr in March to ₹1.37L Cr in May.

insights.title: Food credit grew 94.1% YoY — near upper range
insights.body: Food credit grew 94.1% year-on-year in May 2026, near the upper end of the historical range. Growth re-accelerated 27.7 percentage points (66.4% → 94.1%), reversing April's 25.9 percentage point deceleration and returning to the triple-digit pace last seen in February and March 2026.
insights.implication: April's deceleration was a one-month anomaly. May's 94.1% growth returns food credit to the triple-digit pace seen earlier in 2026, with the absolute book now at ₹1.37L Cr — the highest level in this dataset.

inferences: Food credit grew 94.1% year-on-year in May 2026, up 27.7 percentage points from 66.4% in April.
The May rate matches the February 2026 peak of 94.2% and sits just below the March 2026 high of 92.4%.
The re-acceleration follows April's sharp deceleration, with growth now back near the upper range of 93.2%.

insights.title: Non-food credit at ₹213.8L Cr — new all-time high
insights.body: Non-food credit outstanding reached ₹213.8L Cr in May 2026, the highest level on record. Volume climbed ₹2.7L Cr period-on-period (₹211.1L Cr → ₹213.8L Cr), reversing April's ₹1.8L Cr decline and resuming the upward trajectory from ₹178.1L Cr in January 2025.
insights.implication: The April correction was a brief post-year-end adjustment. May's ₹2.7L Cr gain confirms non-food credit remains in expansion mode, with the book now at its highest level in this dataset.

inferences: Non-food credit rose to ₹213.8L Cr in May 2026, a new peak.
The ₹2.7L Cr monthly gain erased April's post-year-end dip and pushed the book ₹0.9L Cr above the prior March 2026 high of ₹212.9L Cr.
The system has now added ₹35.7L Cr since January 2025, with growth resuming after a one-month pause.

insights.title: Non-food credit added ₹30.8L Cr in FY26 — highest annual add
insights.body: Banks deployed ₹30.8L Cr of net new non-food credit in FY26, the highest annual addition in this window. This figure has remained constant at ₹30.8L Cr across all nine periods, as it reflects the full-year tally locked at March 2026 year-end.
insights.implication: Non-food credit drove the FY26 expansion, with ₹30.8L Cr deployed across agriculture, industry, services, and retail. The book now stands at ₹213.8L Cr in May 2026, the highest level in this dataset.

inferences: Banks added ₹30.8L Cr of net new non-food credit in FY26, the largest annual deployment on record.
This is a full-year metric set at March 2026 and does not change month to month.
The ₹30.8L Cr add represents the system's total net non-food credit expansion over the twelve months ending March 2026.

insights.title: Non-food credit grew 17.4% YoY — fastest in nine periods
insights.body: Non-food credit grew 17.4% year-on-year in May 2026, the fastest rate in this nine-period window. Growth re-accelerated 1.5 percentage points (15.8% → 17.4%), reversing April's 1.1 percentage point deceleration and reaching a new high above the prior March 2026 peak of 16.9%.
insights.implication: April's deceleration was a one-month blip. May's 17.4% growth is the fastest in this dataset, with non-food credit now expanding at a pace not seen in the prior eight periods.

inferences: Non-food credit grew 17.4% year-on-year in May 2026, the fastest rate in nine periods.
Growth re-accelerated 1.5 percentage points from 15.8% in April, erasing the prior month's slowdown.
The May rate now exceeds the March 2026 peak of 16.9%, confirming the credit cycle is still accelerating.

insights.title: All 4 main sectors grew YoY — breadth unchanged
insights.body: All four main credit sectors — agriculture, industry, services, retail — posted positive year-on-year growth in May 2026. Breadth has held at 4 out of 4 sectors for the entire nine-period window, with no sector slipping into contraction.
insights.implication: Credit expansion remains broad-based, with all four main sectors growing in every period since January 2025. The sustained breadth signals strong borrower demand and lending appetite across agriculture, industry, services, and retail.

inferences: All four main credit sectors posted positive year-on-year growth in May 2026.
Breadth has remained at 4 out of 4 sectors across all nine periods in this dataset.
No sector has slipped into contraction since January 2025, indicating broad-based credit expansion.

insights.title: Agriculture share steady at 12.36% — near median
insights.body: Agriculture's share of total bank credit stands at 12.36% in May 2026. Share slipped 0.09pp from 12.44% last period, holding near the median of its nine-period range (12.3%–12.5%).
insights.implication: Agriculture holds a steady 12.4% slice of the book, unchanged in character from the prior period. The sector is neither gaining nor losing ground — lenders face no rebalancing pressure.

inferences: Agriculture's share is 12.36%, down 0.09pp from 12.44% last period.
The move is within the typical 0.5pp noise band and keeps the sector near the middle of its historical range.
Agriculture maintains a stable footprint in the credit mix — proportional growth with no structural shift.

insights.title: Agriculture credit at 14.91% YoY — re-accelerating
insights.body: Agriculture credit grew 14.91% YoY in May 2026, up from 13.70% last period. Growth re-accelerated 1.21pp from 13.70% to 14.91%, reversing the prior period's deceleration and climbing back above the 75th percentile (14.3%).
insights.implication: Agriculture lending has bounced back from the Apr 2026 dip — the re-acceleration to 14.91% confirms the prior slowdown was a pause, not a trend break. The sector remains in a strong growth phase.

inferences: Agriculture credit grew 14.91% YoY, up 1.21pp from 13.70% last period.
The prior period saw a 1.92pp deceleration from the Mar 2026 peak of 15.62%; this period reverses that move.
The sector is back in the upper range of its window, signaling sustained momentum rather than a cooling trend.

insights.title: Industry credit grew 8.2% in FY25, 15.0% in FY26 — 6.8pp step-up
insights.body: Industry credit grew 8.2% in FY25 and 15.0% in FY26, marking a 6.8-point acceleration. The full-year acceleration, measured at Mar 2026 year-end, reflects a near-doubling of annual growth momentum from the prior fiscal year.
insights.implication: Industry credit has completed a full-year breakout — the 6.8pp acceleration is the strongest on record and confirms a capex-driven recovery is entrenched. This is the most compelling industrial lending opportunity in years.

inferences: Industry credit grew 8.2% in FY25 and 15.0% in FY26, a 6.8pp step-up.
This is the largest annual acceleration in the dataset, confirming a structural shift in industrial lending.
The sector has broken out of its multi-year slowdown into a capex-driven recovery.

insights.title: Industry share at 21.63% — edging up from low
insights.body: Industry accounts for 21.63% of total bank credit in May 2026. Share rose 0.13pp from 21.50% last period, climbing off the bottom of its range (21.5%–21.9%) but remaining near the median.
insights.implication: Industry is recovering share after hitting the bottom of its range last period — the 0.13pp gain is small but directionally positive. The sector is in a strong growth phase but not yet reshaping the credit mix.

inferences: Industry's share is 21.63%, up 0.13pp from 21.50% last period.
The prior period marked the lowest level in this window; this period shows a modest recovery.
Industry is growing fast but not yet displacing retail or services as the dominant driver of the credit mix.

insights.title: Industry credit at 17.55% YoY — new high
insights.body: Industry credit grew 17.55% YoY in May 2026, the fastest rate in this nine-period window. Growth accelerated 2.49pp from 15.06% to 17.55%, breaking above the prior maximum of 15.62% and reaching a new high.
insights.implication: Industry lending has broken through its prior ceiling — the 17.55% rate is the highest in this window and confirms the capex recovery is accelerating, not plateauing. The sector is in its strongest growth phase on record.

inferences: Industry credit grew 17.55% YoY, up 2.49pp from 15.06% last period.
The prior period held at 15.06%, near the top of the range; this period breaks out to a new maximum.
The trajectory shows sustained acceleration: 8.2% → 12.1% → 13.5% → 15.0% → 15.1% → 17.5% over six periods.

insights.title: Personal loans 32.81% — slipping from peak
insights.body: Personal loans account for 32.81% of total bank credit in May 2026. Share declined 0.16pp from 32.98% last period, slipping from above the 75th percentile (32.9%) back toward the median.
insights.implication: Personal loans have stopped climbing and are slipping from the Apr 2026 peak — the 0.16pp decline suggests the prior period's bounce was temporary. The sector is stabilizing near the middle of its range, not reshaping the mix.

inferences: Personal loans' share is 32.81%, down 0.16pp from 32.98% last period.
The prior period saw a 0.38pp gain that lifted share to the top of the range; this period reverses part of that move.
Personal loans are giving back ground after a brief bounce, suggesting the rebalancing toward productive sectors may be resuming.

insights.title: Personal loans 15.38% YoY — easing from peak
insights.body: Personal loans credit grew 15.38% YoY in May 2026, down from 16.01% last period. Growth decelerated 0.64pp from 16.01% to 15.38%, slipping from above the 75th percentile (15.7%) toward the median.
insights.implication: Personal loans are decelerating from the Apr 2026 peak — the 15.38% rate is still solid but no longer at the top of the range. The sector may be plateauing after a strong run; unsecured exposure warrants monitoring as growth stabilizes.

inferences: Personal loans grew 15.38% YoY, down 0.64pp from 16.01% last period.
The prior period held at 16.01%, near the top of the range; this period shows a modest slowdown.
The sector remains in mid-teens growth but is no longer at the upper bound of its window.

insights.title: Services credit grew 12.0% in FY25, 19.0% in FY26 — 7.0pp step-up
insights.body: Services credit grew 12.0% in FY25 and 19.0% in FY26, marking a 7.0-point acceleration. The full-year acceleration, measured at Mar 2026 year-end, is 7.0pp — the sharpest annual step-up in this dataset.
insights.implication: Services credit has completed a full-year breakout — the 7.0pp acceleration is the strongest on record and confirms a structural shift, not a temporary spike. The sector is in its most compelling growth phase in years.

inferences: Services credit grew 12.0% in FY25 and 19.0% in FY26, a 7.0pp step-up.
This is the largest annual acceleration on record, confirming a structural shift in services lending.
The sector is in its strongest cycle in recent years, driven by NBFCs, trade, and other sub-sectors.

insights.title: Services share 28.28% — holding upper range
insights.body: Services account for 28.28% of total bank credit in May 2026. Share rose 0.07pp from 28.21% last period, holding above the 75th percentile (28.2%) and near the top of its range.
insights.implication: Services have stabilized near the top of their range after the Apr 2026 dip — the 28.28% share confirms the sector is still capturing a larger slice of the pool than a year ago. The sector remains a dominant force in the credit mix.

inferences: Services' share is 28.28%, up 0.07pp from 28.21% last period.
The prior period saw a 0.26pp decline from the Mar 2026 peak of 28.47%; this period stabilizes near the upper bound.
Services remain a dominant force in the credit mix, holding near the top of their range despite the prior period's pullback.

insights.title: Services credit at 20.4% YoY — highest in this dataset
insights.body: Services credit grew 20.4% year-on-year in May 2026, the highest reading in this nine-period dataset. Growth accelerated from 18.6% in April 2026 to 20.4% in May 2026, a 1.82-point jump. The trajectory over the past year shows: 12.0% → 15.5% → 16.3% → 19.0% → 18.6% → 20.4%.
insights.implication: The April deceleration was a false signal — services credit has re-accelerated to 20.4%, breaking the prior high and confirming the sector's momentum is intact. This is the fastest growth in the dataset, driven by broad-based strength across sub-sectors.

inferences: Services credit grew 20.4% year-on-year in May 2026, the highest reading in this nine-period dataset and 1.82 points above the prior period's 18.6%.
The prior period showed the first deceleration after a sustained run-up; this period's re-acceleration to 20.4% confirms that March's 19.0% peak was not the ceiling.
Services credit is now growing faster than at any point in the past year, with momentum strengthening rather than plateauing.

insights.title: Large corporates at 67.3% share — down 3.8pp in 15 months
insights.body: Large corporates account for 67.3% of industry credit in May 2026, up 0.11pp from the prior period. Share compressed from 71.0% in Jan 2025 to 66.8% in Jan 2026, then stabilised at 67.1% → 67.2% → 67.2% → 67.3% over the last four periods — a net loss of 3.7 percentage points since Jan 2025.
insights.implication: Large corporates have lost 3.7 percentage points of industry credit in 15 months and are now holding steady at 67.3%. The four-period plateau signals the share erosion has paused, but the segment is no longer capturing the bulk of incremental credit — that flow is going to Micro & Small borrowers.

inferences: Large corporates hold 67.3% of industry credit, up 0.11pp from last period but down 3.7pp from 71.0% in Jan 2025.
The share has plateaued at 67.1%–67.3% for four consecutive periods after a sharp 4.2pp drop from Jan 2025 to Jan 2026.
The structural loss confirms incremental credit is flowing disproportionately to MSME borrowers, not large corporates.

insights.title: Large corporates hit 14.4% YoY — fastest in this window
insights.body: Large corporate credit grew 14.4% YoY in May 2026, the strongest reading in this nine-period window. Growth accelerated from 10.0% last period to 14.4%, extending a recovery that began at 5.5% in Jan 2026. The trajectory is 6.8% → 5.6% → 6.9% → 7.5% → 5.5% → 7.8% → 9.1% → 10.0% → 14.4%.
insights.implication: Large corporates are re-accelerating and have hit the fastest growth rate in this window at 14.4%. The 8.9-point gain from Jan 2026 is a sharp recovery. However, the segment is still losing share because MSME growth remains structurally higher — the 14.4% pace is healthy but insufficient to defend market position.

inferences: Large corporate credit grew 14.4% YoY, up from 10.0% last period and the fastest in this nine-period window.
The segment has re-accelerated from a low of 5.5% in Jan 2026, gaining 8.9 percentage points in four periods.
Despite the acceleration, large corporates are losing share because MSME segments are growing faster — Micro & Small at 26.2%, Medium at 21.2%.

insights.title: Medium enterprises at 9.7% share — flat for five periods
insights.body: Medium enterprises account for 9.7% of industry credit in May 2026, down 0.05pp from the prior period. Share rose from 8.9% in Jan 2025 to 9.7% by Jan 2026 and has held at 9.7% for five consecutive periods — a net gain of 0.8 percentage points since Jan 2025.
insights.implication: Medium enterprises have carved out a 9.7% share and are holding it. The five-period plateau confirms the segment is growing in line with industry credit, not capturing outsized incremental flow. The 0.8pp gain from Jan 2025 to Jan 2026 was a one-time structural shift, now complete.

inferences: Medium enterprises hold 9.7% of industry credit, unchanged for five straight periods after rising from 8.9% in Jan 2025.
The five-period plateau signals the segment is growing in line with the broader industry pool, not outpacing it.
The 0.8pp gain from Jan 2025 to Jan 2026 was a structural shift, but the segment has since stabilised.

insights.title: Medium enterprises at 21.2% YoY — re-accelerating
insights.body: Medium enterprise credit grew 21.2% YoY in May 2026, up 1.29pp from the prior period. Growth re-accelerated from 19.9% last period to 21.2%, after decelerating from a peak of 22.3% in Jan 2026. The trajectory is 18.4% → 18.0% → 18.5% → 20.4% → 22.3% → 21.0% → 21.8% → 19.9% → 21.2%.
insights.implication: Medium enterprises are re-accelerating after a brief deceleration. The 21.2% pace is healthy and far ahead of large corporates, but the segment is not the fastest-growing — Micro & Small at 26.2% is outpacing it. The re-acceleration confirms Medium remains a strong outperformer, but momentum is concentrating in smaller borrowers.

inferences: Medium enterprise credit grew 21.2% YoY, up from 19.9% last period and re-accelerating after a two-period deceleration.
The segment peaked at 22.3% in Jan 2026, dipped to 19.9% in Apr 2026, and has now recovered to 21.2%.
The 21.2% pace is far ahead of large corporates at 14.4% but below Micro & Small at 26.2%.

insights.title: Micro & Small grew 32.7% in FY26 vs 8.9% in FY25 — 23.8pp step-up
insights.body: Micro & Small credit grew 8.9% in the year ending Mar 2025 and 32.7% in the year ending Mar 2026, a 23.8 percentage point acceleration. Full-year growth jumped from 8.9% in FY25 to 32.7% in FY26 — the sharpest year-over-year step-up in this dataset.
insights.implication: This is the defining inflection in industry credit. Micro & Small lending has entered a new growth regime, and the 23.8pp step-up from FY25 to FY26 is unprecedented in this dataset. Banks and NBFCs scaling this segment are capturing outsized share of incremental credit.

inferences: Micro & Small credit grew 8.9% in FY25 and 32.7% in FY26, a 23.8 percentage point acceleration.
The 23.8pp step-up is the largest full-year acceleration in this dataset, confirming a structural inflection.
Lenders with exposure to Micro & Small are riding the fastest-growing segment in industry credit.

insights.title: Micro & Small at 23.1% share — up 3.1pp in 14 months
insights.body: Micro & Small enterprises account for 23.1% of industry credit in May 2026, down 0.06pp from the prior period. Share surged from 20.0% in Mar 2025 to 23.5% in Jan 2026, then eased to 23.1% → 23.2% → 23.1% → 23.1% → 23.1% over the last five periods — a net gain of 3.1 percentage points since Mar 2025.
insights.implication: Micro & Small borrowers are capturing share at the expense of large corporates. The 3.1pp gain in 14 months is a structural reallocation, not noise. The five-period plateau at 23.1% signals the segment is now growing in line with the broader pool, having completed a sharp share grab from Mar 2025 to Jan 2026.

inferences: Micro & Small borrowers hold 23.1% of industry credit, down 0.06pp from last period but up 3.1pp from 20.0% in Mar 2025.
The share peaked at 23.5% in Jan 2026 and has since stabilised at 23.1%–23.2% for five consecutive periods.
The 3.1pp gain in 14 months is a structural reallocation, coming at the expense of large corporates who lost 3.7pp over the same window.

insights.title: Micro & Small at 26.2% YoY — decelerating but still fastest
insights.body: Micro & Small credit grew 26.2% YoY in May 2026, down 3.91pp from the prior period. Growth decelerated from 30.1% last period to 26.2%, after peaking at 32.7% in Mar 2026. The trajectory is 9.6% → 9.6% → 8.9% → 31.0% → 31.2% → 30.4% → 32.7% → 30.1% → 26.2%.
insights.implication: Micro & Small is decelerating but remains the hottest segment in industry credit. The 6.5-point drop from the Mar 2026 peak is notable, but the 26.2% pace is still far ahead of all other segments. The deceleration is worth watching — if growth drops below 20%, the segment risks losing its share-gaining momentum.

inferences: Micro & Small credit grew 26.2% YoY, down from 30.1% last period and the slowest since the segment exploded from 8.9% in Mar 2025.
The segment peaked at 32.7% in Mar 2026 and has now decelerated for two consecutive periods, losing 6.5 percentage points.
Despite the deceleration, 26.2% is still the fastest growth rate in industry credit — ahead of Medium at 21.2% and Large at 14.4%.

insights.title: MSME-Large spread at 11.8pp — narrowest since Mar 2025
insights.body: MSME credit is growing 11.8 percentage points faster than large corporate credit in May 2026. The spread narrowed from 20.1pp last period to 11.8pp, the smallest gap since 2.1pp in Mar 2025. The trajectory is 2.8pp → 4.0pp → 2.1pp → 23.5pp → 25.7pp → 22.6pp → 23.5pp → 20.1pp → 11.8pp.
insights.implication: The growth divergence between MSME and large corporates is narrowing sharply. Large corporates are re-accelerating and closing the gap, but MSME segments are still growing nearly twice as fast. The 11.8pp spread is the narrowest since the MSME surge began, signaling large corporates are regaining momentum — but incremental credit is still flowing disproportionately to smaller borrowers.

inferences: The MSME-Large growth spread is 11.8 percentage points, down from 20.1pp last period and the narrowest since Mar 2025.
The spread peaked at 25.7pp in Jan 2026 and has now narrowed for three consecutive periods, losing 13.9 points.
The narrowing is driven by large corporates re-accelerating to 14.4% while Micro & Small decelerated to 26.2%.

insights.title: Housing Finance Companies holds 17.7% of NBFC credit; Public Financial Institutions 17.0%
insights.body: RBI breaks NBFC credit into two sub-categories. Housing Finance Companies holds 17.7% and Public Financial Institutions 17.0% — these are size shares, not growth rates. Together the two break-outs cover 34.7% of NBFC credit; the rest is not sub-classified in the RBI statement.
insights.implication: Read this as size mix, not momentum: the two blocks are close in size — a move in either shifts NBFC credit. Check the matching growth scan before positioning.

inferences: Housing Finance Companies is the larger break-out at 17.7% of NBFC credit.
Public Financial Institutions holds 17.0% — a 0.7 percentage points gap between the only two break-outs.
Together they cover 34.7% of NBFC credit; RBI does not sub-classify the rest.

insights.title: Public Financial Institutions growing at 71.8% YoY; Housing Finance Companies at 19.7%
insights.body: Public Financial Institutions grew 71.8% year-on-year against Housing Finance Companies at 19.7% — a 52.0 percentage points growth gap between the two sub-categories RBI breaks out.
insights.implication: Lenders can lean into Public Financial Institutions (71.8%) and monitor Housing Finance Companies (19.7%). Broad participation supports diversified deployment.

inferences: Public Financial Institutions is the faster of the two at 71.8% YoY.
Housing Finance Companies is at 19.7% — 52.0 percentage points behind.
Both are growing — the gap is about pace, not direction.

insights.title: Services credit mix rotating toward Non-Banking Financial Companies (+3.43 pp share in a year)
insights.body: Compared with the same month a year ago, the biggest share gains in services credit came from Non-Banking Financial Companies +3.43 pp; Computer Software +0.19 pp; Aviation +0.04 pp. The ground came from Other Services -2.13 pp; Trade -0.60 pp; Transport Operators -0.56 pp. In all, 3.72 pp of the mix changed hands. The gains concentrate in financial intermediation, the cessions in trade & distribution — the mix is tilting toward financial intermediation.
insights.implication: This is a composition read: it says where the mix is shifting, not why and not what happens next. The tilt toward financial intermediation is the line to watch — confirm it holds next month before treating it as a trend.

inferences: Each segment's share of services credit is compared with the same month a year earlier — the change is in percentage points of the mix.
Top gainer: Non-Banking Financial Companies at +3.43 pp. Biggest cession: Other Services at -2.13 pp.
Rotation mass — the share that changed hands — is 3.72 pp.
The gains concentrate in financial intermediation, the cessions in trade & distribution — the mix is tilting toward financial intermediation.

insights.title: Non-Banking Financial Companies is the biggest slice of services credit at 34.5%
insights.body: Non-Banking Financial Companies holds the largest share of services credit at 34.5%, Trade 22.5%; Shipping is the smallest at 0.2%. These are size shares, not growth rates. Top three hold 77.3% of services credit, spread 34.4 percentage points.
insights.implication: Composition, not momentum: Non-Banking Financial Companies carries the most weight of services credit. Concentration means the big blocks drive the category — watch them first.

inferences: Non-Banking Financial Companies is the largest block at 34.5% of services credit.
Shipping is the smallest at 0.2% — a 34.4 percentage points spread across 10 sub-categories.
